R1_instruction_following.criterion: A refused publish shows its reason beside the poster in question, naming the missing written alternative.
R1_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if the message sits next to the poster in the studio editor and says the written alternative is missing. No if the message appears only as a page-level banner, or if the missing field is unnamed.
R1_instruction_following.rationale: The app correctly supplies a refusal reason that can name the missing written alternative, but all publish failures are routed to a general RECORD-form alert in the editor's left column. Poster rows are in the separate MEDIA column and contain only thumbnail, role/dimensions, and alt text. Therefore the required message does not sit beside the poster in question, so the criterion fails under the explicit evaluation rule.
evidence:
The delivered studio editor template (`templates/studio/edit.html`) has only one publish/save `role="alert"` bound to `error`: `

` inside the RECORD form in the left `.edit-col`, before the PUBLISHING section. The poster rows are rendered separately in `

    ` inside the MEDIA section in the second `.edit-col`; there is no per-poster publish error element.

The delivered client (`static/site.js`, `editForm.publish`) catches a refused publish and assigns the server message to the general `self.error`, which is the left-column record-form alert—not to `mediaError` or a particular poster row.

The server's missing-alt refusal does name the field: `The poster needs a written alternative before this record can be published` (`cirrus/app.py`). Thus naming is implemented, but placement beside the poster is not.

The running editor at `/studio/items/4ab38ee158df705fdc1ab56a83865592` demonstrated the actual placement mechanism after PUBLISH was refused: the alert `A record needs a poster before it can be published` appeared between DISCIPLINE and SAVE in the RECORD area, while MEDIA was a separate section/column. This directly confirms publish errors use the page/record-level alert rather than a message adjacent to the poster.
CSS confirms the geometry: `.edit-columns { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 64px; }`; the general error and poster/media list therefore occupy separate columns at desktop width.

R2_instruction_following.criterion: The refusal a signed-up account meets at the studio reads as a deliberate decision rather than as something going wrong.
R2_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader is returned to a working public surface that says in the house's own voice that the studio is not theirs. No if the refusal reads as an error, a dead end, or a half-drawn studio the reader is left standing in.
R2_instruction_following.rationale: The signed-up account is returned to a functional public surface rather than an error or half-rendered studio, but that surface does not say in the house's voice that the studio is not theirs. The refusal is therefore an unexplained redirect, so the explicit evaluation rule is not met.
evidence: Constructed the required state through the visible flow: opened `/studio/login`, followed the `Sign up` link, created a new account, and was returned to the working public home page.

While the new signed-up viewer account was active, directly requesting `/studio` ended at `/` (HTTP 200 public home). The resulting screen showed the normal Cirrus navigation and work tiles, but no refusal notice and no copy saying that the studio is for the house's producers or is not this account's.
Requesting `/studio/login` with that same viewer account likewise redirected to `/` without an explanatory notice.

Delivered source corroborates the observed route: `cirrus/pages.py` `_guard()` redirects any authenticated non-producer to `/`, and `studio_login()` also redirects an authenticated viewer to `/`; neither route supplies refusal messaging.

R3_instruction_following.criterion: On the studio palette each record shows its own state in words beside its title.
R3_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if each row states whether the record is live or held back, in words. No if the state is carried by a colour, an icon or a position alone.
R3_instruction_following.rationale: The complete studio record set was reached and directly inspected. Every record communicates publication state using visible words—LIVE for published and UNLISTED for held back—both on the cards and in the opened palette rows, adjacent to the record title within the same row/card. Although live cards also add a small square marker, the written label remains present, so state is not conveyed by colour, icon, or position alone.
evidence: Authenticated at /studio as producer@example.com and inspected the complete Records grid. Every one of the 35 visible record links in the browser snapshot has an accessible name ending in an explicit word state: either “LIVE” or “UNLISTED” (for example, “Rives … TALENT LIVE,” “Noor Vasquez … TALENT UNLISTED,” “The Halo … WORK LIVE,” and “The Quiet Room … WORK UNLISTED”).
The full-page screenshot directly shows both state variants written on the record cards: LIVE and UNLISTED. Thus held-back records are not represented only by an icon, colour, or position.

Opened the command palette and directly observed each result row carry the same state in words beside the title; examples include “Rives … LIVE” and “Noor Vasquez … UNLISTED.” The viewport screenshot shows these as title and right-side state columns on the same row.

Measured palette result buttons: each is 1198×49 px and uses CSS grid columns `90px 738px 200px 90px`, placing the title and textual state in the same row. Both sampled live and held-back rows were visible with opacity 1.
Inspected rendered HTML for representative records of both kinds and both entity types. Each contains a `` with literal text `LIVE` or `UNLISTED`; palette rows likewise contain `LIVE/UNLISTED`.

Delivered template `templates/studio/palette.html` renders this state for every iterated record as `{{ 'LIVE' if it.published else 'UNLISTED' }}`, and the palette script maps every record to `stateLabel: r.published ? "LIVE" : "UNLISTED"`.

R4_ux_flow.criterion: The page that follows a publish reads as an ending rather than as another form.
R4_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if the confirmation is composed in the house's own register and offers one onward move. No if it is a bare success screen, or if it puts the publish control back in front of a producer who has just used it.
R4_ux_flow.rationale: The observed post-publish destination is a tailored editorial confirmation, not a bare success message or another form. It names the record, states that it is live, gives its public address and discipline, and provides one clear onward workflow move back to the palette without re-presenting the publish control.
evidence: Completed the producer flow directly: signed in at /studio/login, opened the unlisted talent “Probe Talent 76b38ec23fd2,” attached a valid 640×800 poster with written alternative text, and selected PUBLISH.
The publish action navigated to /studio/items/f403323f12fb87491644a4ee8b3c8da8/published rather than returning to the edit form.

R5_ux_flow.criterion: The studio's first screen presents the palette as the way work is done rather than as one control among a page of chrome.
R5_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if a producer arriving at the studio can see that typing is the next thing to do. No if the palette shares the screen with a toolbar, a sidebar or a dashboard that competes with it for the first move.
R5_ux_flow.rationale: The evaluation rule explicitly says No when the palette shares the first screen with a toolbar, sidebar, or dashboard that competes for the first move. The authenticated studio landing screen includes global navigation and a prominent records dashboard, and its palette is initially only a button rather than a ready-to-type input. Direct interaction confirmed typing does not engage it until the producer clicks the command control. Therefore the requirement is not met.
evidence: After signing in as producer@example.com and arriving at /studio, the first screen showed a full dashboard: global WORKS/TALENTS/CONTACT/ABOUT navigation, a COMMAND button, a RECORDS heading, and a large multi-column grid of talent/work record cards filling the viewport.

On initial arrival there was no text input in the interactive-element snapshot; the palette entry point was a button labeled “COMMAND — TYPE TO SEARCH THE HOUSE'S RECORDS AND ACTIONS.” Pressing the letter “r” at that first screen did nothing and left the page unchanged.

The captured 1440×900 viewport visibly shows the records dashboard competing with the command affordance, rather than the palette being presented as the sole or dominant way work is done.

R6_ux_flow.evaluation_rule: Yes if the create route carries the site's own frame, type and restraint. No if it is set in a default form style, or if its chrome is unrelated to the chrome a visitor sees.
R6_ux_flow.rationale: The create route demonstrably belongs to the same house: it uses the public site's shared frame, proprietary Cirrus display/text fonts, two-color palette, spacing, and deliberately minimal controls. The end-to-end form interaction—including invalid submission feedback and successful unlisted creation—worked within that same visual system. It does not appear as a default or unrelated admin form.

The running create route visibly retains the same visitor-facing frame as / and /about: lowercase Cirrus wordmark at top left; WORKS centered; TALENTS, CONTACT, and ABOUT at top right; the same pale ground/dark ink; and the same bottom-right house credit glyph.

The create screen uses the site's own typography and restrained visual vocabulary rather than browser-default form styling: a large light-weight Cirrus display face for “New talent,” Cirrus Text at 12px for navigation, labels, inputs, and controls, thin dark one-pixel rules, transparent control backgrounds, generous whitespace, and only the site's dark/light palette.

Direct computed styles on the running create route showed the navigation, input, and CREATE TALENT control using `Cirrus Text`, with 12px text and transparent backgrounds; the page heading visually uses the same editorial display face seen throughout the public site.

Compared directly with the public /about route in the same 1440×900 viewport: both surfaces use the identical fixed wordmark/navigation/credit frame, pale ground, dark ink, display/interface type pairing, and spacious composition. The studio content reads as a restrained extension within that frame, not unrelated admin chrome.

Completed the create form flow and checked validation timing: submitting the untouched form kept the user on /studio/talents/new and immediately exposed the inline role=alert message “A title is required.” After entering reversible fixture title “R6 House Form 260322” and submitting, the app created it unlisted and navigated to `/studio/items/d12bddc4816939581145f23aa96f23ca`, where the confirmation state identified `TALENT / R6-HOUSE-FORM-260322`, the title, and `UNLISTED`.

Delivered templates corroborate the live observation: `templates/studio/new.html` extends `base.html`, while `base.html` owns the same wordmark, WORKS/TALENTS/CONTACT/ABOUT navigation, marks, credit, cursor pair, and contact overlay used by public routes. The studio therefore literally mounts inside the site's shared frame.

R7_functionality.criterion: A drained still on the public work index reads as a deliberate treatment rather than as a picture still arriving.
R7_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the resting index reads as a composed page of colourless photographs. No if a drained still is indistinguishable from a placeholder, a broken image or a loading state.
R7_functionality.rationale: The public work index clearly presents composed, labelled monochrome imagery at rest. Direct hover/leave observation shows colour is intentionally removed and restored, while the successful JPEG response and stable intrinsic dimensions distinguish the still from loading, placeholder, or broken-image states.
evidence: On the public /works index, the resting Sonder tile was visibly rendered as a detailed dark monochrome gradient/grain photograph, with its ordinal/title composition; it did not resemble a blank placeholder, broken-image icon, or loading spinner.

Moving the pointer onto Sonder visibly returned its muted green colour, and moving away drained it back to monochrome. This reversible state change directly establishes that the colourless resting appearance is an intentional treatment.

Computed/source styling confirms the treatment: `.tile-still` uses `filter: saturate(0)` at rest, while `.entry-row:hover .tile-still` and focus-within switch to `saturate(1)` over an 0.8s transition.

The served media endpoint for the observed still returned HTTP 200 with `content-type: image/jpeg` and 7,362 bytes, ruling out a broken image response. The template also reserves its exact 300×300 aspect ratio, while the observed element was fully visible at 300×300.

The media implementation renders a deterministic two-gradient field with vignette and grain. Thus the visible tonal detail is authored media content underneath a deliberate CSS desaturation, not a loading skeleton.

R8_ui_visual.criterion: On the entry cluster, the work index and the roster alike the two grounds read as a matched warm pair rather than as black on white.
R8_ui_visual.evaluation_rule: Yes if the dark surface reads as warmed toward red and the pale one as warmed toward green, and the site never reads as neutral grey. No if the pair reads as pure black and pure white, or as two unrelated temperatures.
R8_ui_visual.rationale: The entry cluster uses the red-warmed near-black ground and pale green-warmed ink, while both the work index and roster reverse that exact shared pair. Screenshots confirm the visual relationship across all three required surfaces, and measured styles plus the shared CSS variables establish that the grounds are deliberately chromatic rather than neutral black/white or unrelated temperatures.
evidence: Entry route `/` screenshot shows the full 1440×900 entry cluster on a dark ground. Measured entry navigation and cluster-link ink is `rgb(233, 234, 228)`, and the measured first cluster still occupies `x=62, y=88, width=300, height=161`, confirming the measurement applies to visible entry content rather than an off-screen artifact.

Works index `/works` screenshot shows the index on the pale ground. Measured WORKS navigation and a work tile link use `rgb(6, 4, 3)` ink; the measured first tile link is `x=40, y=900, width=598, height=320`.

Delivered stylesheet `static/app.css` defines the shared pair as `--color-dark: #060403` and `--color-light: #e9eae4`; `body` uses the light ground with dark ink, while `body.is-dark` reverses them. `templates/base.html` applies `is-dark` specifically to the entry route.

The numeric channels establish the intended temperature relationship: dark `#060403` = RGB(6,4,3), with red highest; pale `#e9eae4` = RGB(233,234,228), with green highest. Neither is pure black/white nor a neutral equal-channel grey.

R10_motion.criterion: A link on a public route is recognisable as a link by a reader whose pointer stays parked.
R10_motion.evaluation_rule: Yes if position, setting and grouping make what is pressable legible at rest. No if finding what is pressable requires sweeping the pointer, or if a colour is what marks it.
R10_motion.rationale: The home page exposes a plainly conventional header navigation at rest. Its position, vocabulary, and grouping make `WORKS` recognisable as a link while the pointer remains parked, and pressing it confirms the affordance. Color is not the sole marker.
evidence: On the public home route `/`, with the pointer left parked, the at-rest viewport visibly presented `WORKS`, `TALENTS`, `CONTACT`, and `ABOUT` together as a conventional top navigation group, plus the `cirrus` home mark at the opposite top corner.

The `WORKS` item occupied a stable top-navigation position (x=696, y=28, 47×14), alongside `TALENTS` (x=1158), `CONTACT` (x=1255), and `ABOUT` (x=1357); this placement and grouping identify the controls without pointer exploration.

Inspection confirmed the visible `WORKS` item is an anchor with `href='/works'`. Using keyboard press/Enter while it was focused navigated successfully from `/` to the public `/works` route, directly confirming that the at-rest navigation label is pressable.

The links had no underline (`text-decoration-line: none`), but recognisability did not depend on a unique link color: the semantic navigation words, fixed header placement, and grouping supplied the affordance. Keyboard focus additionally showed a clear 2px outline, though hover was never needed to discover the item.
CDP motion capture was started immediately before the Enter press and stopped after the destination appeared; the route changed to `/works`, confirming the required press interaction.

R11_functionality.criterion: The about route's blur reads as attached to the reader's hand rather than as an effect played at them.
R11_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the sharpening tracks the wheel continuously and stops where the reader stops. No if it advances in steps, runs ahead of the scroll, or leaves text unreadable once the reader has stopped moving.
R11_functionality.rationale: The live interaction and settled screenshots show that sharpening follows scroll position in both directions and remains fixed once scrolling settles. The source corroborates that blur is a continuous function of current geometry, not a staged or autonomous animation, so it reads as attached to the reader’s scrolling hand.
evidence: On /about at a 1280×800 viewport, direct wheel scrolling through several distances showed the blur changing continuously with each new scroll position: the opening figure blurred further as it moved away, the first body paragraph sharpened near the viewport middle, and the long “Founded in Paris…” paragraph sharpened when it reached the middle.

After scrolling stopped with “Founded in Paris…” near the viewport center and waiting, a second screenshot remained at the same settled position with that paragraph fully crisp; the effect did not continue playing or leave the centered text unreadable.

Reversing upward by 180px made the first body paragraph readable while re-blurring the lower paragraph; subsequent smaller downward movements of 70px and 90px progressively moved sharpness back to the lower paragraph, demonstrating reversibility and position-dependent tracking rather than stepped advancement.

Delivered source confirms the observed mechanism: `initBlur()` calculates each target’s distance from the viewport midpoint and directly assigns `filter: blur(...)`; it is registered with the shared scroll source, recomputed via requestAnimationFrame, and has no independent duration/timeline. Smooth wheel scrolling calls `applyScroll(smoothState.current)` every animation frame and stops exactly when current reaches the wheel target.

R12_accessibility.criterion: Under a reduced-motion preference the about route still reads as the designed page rather than as a stripped fallback.
R12_accessibility.evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader loses the effect and nothing else, with the same blocks in the same places. No if the route drops content, shifts its layout, or reads as a plain unstyled version of itself.
R12_accessibility.rationale: The fresh-load A/B capture directly shows that the motion effects are removed under the preference, while the runtime snapshot, full-page rendering, and shared template/CSS demonstrate that all designed blocks remain present and composed in the same layout. The about route therefore loses the effect and nothing structural or stylistic essential.
evidence: On `/about`, a fresh load with `prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference` produced 113 captured CSS animations, primarily 300ms opacity and 450ms transform animations with staggered delays.
After setting `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and reloading, the same capture produced only one incidental 200ms opacity animation; the large staggered transform/opacity motion set was absent.

The reduced-motion accessibility snapshot retained the complete designed content and chrome: wordmark/navigation, the full headline figure with seven CIRRUS lines, both about-copy blocks, the composed CIRRUS/PROD/FOR/ITS/AND/PICTURE/MAKERS lockup, four-column footer content, contact overlay, and active ABOUT state.

The reduced-motion full-page screenshot showed the same composed serif typography, centered figure, positioned marks, copy blocks, lockup, generous spacing, and gradient-backed four-column footer—not a plain or unstyled fallback.

Delivered source corroborates that reduced motion changes effects rather than structure: `templates/about.html` has one shared set of figure, body, lockup, and footer blocks; `static/site.js` makes blur `filter:none` under reduced motion and uses native scrolling; the reduced-motion CSS disables transitions and forces existing reveal/split/blur content into its completed visible state rather than hiding or reflowing it.

R13_accessibility.criterion: The focus ring is legible on the pale ground, on the dark ground and over a photograph alike.
R13_accessibility.evaluation_rule: Yes if a keyboard reader can find the focused control on all three surfaces. No if the ring disappears against one of them, or if it reads as a browser default dropped onto a considered page.
R13_accessibility.rationale: Keyboard testing directly exercised controls on the pale and dark themes and photographic controls. In every required context the focused control was visually findable, using an intentional, theme-adaptive 2px solid ring with spacing from the control rather than an unstyled browser-default indicator. This verifies the requested surfaces without claiming broader WCAG conformance.
evidence: On the pale `/talents` surface, keyboard focus on the DIRECTOR filter produced a clearly visible dark rectangular indicator; computed style was `outline: 2px solid rgb(6, 4, 3)` with `outline-offset: 3px` against the pale `#e9eae4` ground.

On the dark `/` surface, keyboard focus on the skip link and a project tile produced a clearly visible light indicator; the focused “The Halo” photographic tile measured 300×161px and had `outline: 2px solid rgb(233, 234, 228)` with `outline-offset: 3px`. The screenshot visibly shows the ring around the photographic control against both its image edge and the surrounding black composition.

On the pale `/talents` composition, the photographic portrait link itself was keyboard-focused. A dark 2px outline with 3px offset visibly enclosed the entire 246×330px photograph, making the focused photo control easy to locate.

Delivered CSS explicitly defines a considered focus treatment rather than relying on browser defaults: `a:focus-visible, button:focus-visible, input:focus-visible, select:focus-visible, [tabindex]:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--color-dark); outline-offset: 3px; opacity: 1; }`, with `body.is-dark ... { outline-color: var(--color-light); }`. It also documents that focus is not the hover treatment; hover instead uses reduced opacity.

R14_responsiveness.criterion: The narrow roster reads as the same roster a wide window shows rather than as a different page.
R14_responsiveness.evaluation_rule: Yes if the name setting, the order and the sense of one talent at a time all survive the change. No if the narrow layout reads as a list, a grid or a stack that the wide layout never suggested.
R14_responsiveness.rationale: The narrow breakpoint is recognizably the same interactive roster: identical talent set and traversal order, identical single-active-talent model, and the same name/discipline/portrait/profile/counter composition. It does not turn into a page structure absent from the wide layout.

R15_responsiveness.criterion: A visitor on a phone is shown the work as a colour portfolio, with nothing held behind a gesture that device cannot perform.
R15_responsiveness.evaluation_rule: Yes if everything a pointer would reveal is already present on the narrow layout. No if a caption, a colour or a title is reachable only by a hover on a surface that has no pointer.
R15_responsiveness.rationale: The desktop-only portfolio disclosures are the hover cursor/title treatment and colour return. On the phone breakpoint, titles are rendered as persistent captions and portfolio stills are forced to full saturation. Thus neither a title/caption nor colour is held behind a hover gesture unavailable to a phone visitor.
evidence: At 1440×900 on `/`, hovering the first portfolio tile caused the pointer-only cursor label `THE HALO` to appear; the tile markup also contains an initially hidden `.cluster-caption` with the same title.

At 390×844 on `/`, the rendered narrow layout visibly showed title captions under the image tiles (for example `The Halo`, `Common Ground`, and `The Absolute Shelter`). The first tile measured x=62..362 within the 390px viewport and its link was visible at 300×178.5px.

Delivered CSS directly accounts for the responsive equivalence: desktop `.cluster-caption` starts at `opacity: 0`, while inside the narrow breakpoint (`@media (max-width: 768px), (max-height: 500px)`) it becomes static, displayed, and `opacity: 1`; the pointer cursor is separately disabled for coarse pointers.

At 390×844, the `/works` snapshot exposed all portfolio ordinals and titles 001–013 in visible page text; each measured work link was 342px wide within x=24..366, with no horizontal overflow according to the supplied deterministic measurement (`bodyScrollWidth=390`).

R16_motion.criterion: The fade between two public routes reads as unhurried rather than as the site being slow.
R16_motion.evaluation_rule: Yes if the change reads as one object turning a page. No if the reader is left waiting on a dimmed screen, or if the fade is indistinguishable from a slow response.
R16_motion.rationale: The observed and source-verified behavior is a brief, synchronized 400 ms partial fade followed immediately by route replacement. Because the outgoing interface remains visibly present at roughly 48% opacity and there is no post-fade pause, it reads as one composed object turning a page rather than a dimmed screen waiting on a slow response.
evidence: Directly exercised two public-route changes: `/` → `/talents` and `/talents` → `/about`; both reached the destination normally, with `/about` visibly rendered as “About Cirrus.”

CDP motion capture started immediately before each click. The captures recorded the route-level opacity animations together at the same start time, with 400 ms duration, zero delay, and `ease` timing (for example IDs 1012 and 1013 on Talents → About).

Delivered source confirms a single coordinated treatment: `.frame, .well, .footer { transition: opacity 0.4s; }`, while the leaving state applies the same partial dimming to frame and well: `body.is-leaving .frame, body.is-leaving .well { opacity: 0.482; }`.

Delivered source confirms navigation occurs after exactly 400 ms—the same duration as the fade—via `setTimeout(function () { location.href = a.href; }, 400)`. Thus there is no extra hold after the fade and no ambiguous network-wait interval.

The outgoing page never fades to a blank screen: its opacity bottoms out at 0.482, and the destination replaces it at the end of the brief 400 ms fade. This preserves visible continuity while clearly signaling an intentional page turn.

R17_instruction_following.criterion: A commissioner can tell from any public route how to reach the house, and finds one address rather than a form.
R17_instruction_following.evaluation_rule: Yes if the enquiry channel is findable from the chrome on every route and resolves to the house's own address. No if it is buried on one route only, or if the site asks the reader to fill in fields instead.
R17_instruction_following.rationale: The shared public chrome makes the enquiry channel available from every rendered public page, including detail, account-signup, mobile, and not-found routes. It resolves directly to the one email address `prod@example.com`, which source data identifies as Cirrus's own house contact. No enquiry form is substituted for that address.
evidence: On the public home route `/`, the persistent main navigation visibly includes `CONTACT`; its DOM href is `mailto:prod@example.com`. The same page also exposes `PROD@EXAMPLE.COM` with the identical mailto target.

Direct checks on `/works`, `/talents`, `/about`, `/works/the-halo`, `/signup`, and a public 404 route all showed the same chrome-level `CONTACT` item. On `/talents` and `/signup`, its href was directly verified as `mailto:prod@example.com`; `/about`, `/works`, and the work-detail route also visibly exposed `PROD@EXAMPLE.COM`.

That shared base defines the persistent chrome contact as `CONTACT` and includes the contact overlay, whose sole item is the same `mailto:prod@example.com` address.

Source search for `<form` across top-level public templates found only the `/signup` account-creation form; there is no public enquiry/contact form. The enquiry affordance itself is a direct email address, not a field-based flow.

R18_functionality.criterion: An emptied roster speaks in the house's own register rather than as a system message.
R18_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the sentence reads as written by the house and does not read as a failure. No if it reads as an error string, a placeholder, or a developer's stub.

evidence: Constructed an empty roster at `/talents?discipline=stylist`; the rendered page directly displayed: “There is no published talent in this discipline yet.”

`.

R19_functionality.criterion: A work index caught mid-load looks like the work index rather than like a page being assembled.
R19_functionality.evaluation_rule: Yes if the reserved spaces read as part of the composition, carrying no spinner, no shimmer and no dimensions drawn across them. No if the loading page shows skeleton furniture the finished page never has.
R19_functionality.rationale: The index was directly observed under a constructed in-flight media condition. Its empty media footprint behaved as intentional negative space inside the actual work-row composition, with stable caption/chrome placement and no loading-only furniture. The reserved dimensions match the finished tile but are never drawn as text, so the criterion is met.
evidence: On /works at 1440×900, I delayed every /api/media/ response by 15 seconds, reloaded, and scrolled the first work into view while its image request was still pending. The captured viewport retained the finished index composition: fixed Cirrus/navigation chrome, the editorial opening line, the central Works mark, and the first row’s “001” / “The Halo” caption aligned around the reserved media area. No loading spinner, shimmer, progress text, or pixel-dimension label appeared.

The first work link measured 598×320 during the delayed-media state. Its served markup reserves exactly that area through `<span class="tile-box reveal" data-width="598" data-height="320" style="aspect-ratio:598/320">` and an image with `width="598" height="320"`; dimensions are attributes only and are not rendered across the reserved space.

Computed styling for the work link during inspection reported `animation-name: none` and `background-image: none`. Source searches across all templates found no `spinner`, `shimmer`, `skeleton`, `loading-placeholder`, or dimension-label patterns, and app.css contained no spinner/shimmer/skeleton or `@keyframes` implementation.

After removing the route delay, the same first work link remained 598×320 and populated with its finished still, confirming the pending state reserved the finished tile’s footprint rather than introducing temporary skeleton furniture.

R20_scope_discipline.criterion: The dependency manifest names Flask with its Jinja template layer, Alpine.js, a PostgreSQL driver and a production WSGI server and nothing beside them; no second datastore client, cache client, queue client, object-store SDK, search library, mail library or identity-provider SDK is declared.
R20_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A dependency is a package named in the manifest's runtime dependency block -- requirements.txt, the pyproject project dependencies, or the package.json dependencies -- not a transitive lock entry and not a development-only tool such as a linter, formatter or test runner. The permitted set is Flask, its Jinja template layer, Alpine.js, a PostgreSQL driver and a production WSGI server, together with the direct requirements of those five; a password hashing routine is a direct requirement of the authentication the brief mandates and is never a violation on its own. Yes if every runtime dependency falls inside that set. No if the manifest declares any package outside it -- a second datastore client such as a Redis, MongoDB, SQLite or MySQL driver, a cache client, a task queue, an object-store SDK, a search library, a mail-sending library, an identity-provider or OAuth SDK, or an image-processing, rasterisation, font-tooling, compression or array-computation library standing beside the five.
R20_scope_discipline.rationale: R20 is not satisfied. The runtime manifest directly declares Pillow, which the rule explicitly identifies as a disallowed image-processing library standing beside the permitted stack. In addition, Alpine.js is shipped as a static vendored script rather than named in the dependency manifest. The single disallowed runtime dependency is sufficient to settle this conjunctive criterion as false.
evidence: The delivered source tree contains requirements.txt as the dependency manifest and no pyproject.toml or package.json.
requirements.txt declares: flask, gunicorn, psycopg, markupsafe, blinker, click, itsdangerous, jinja2, werkzeug, pillow, packaging, and typing-extensions.

The manifest therefore includes the required Flask/Jinja/PostgreSQL-driver/production-WSGI stack, but it also directly declares `pillow`, an image-processing library explicitly excluded by the evaluation rule.
Alpine.js is delivered as `/app/static/alpine.min.js` and referenced by `templates/base.html`, but it is not named in requirements.txt.

Dockerfile independently installs the same direct runtime package set and describes Pillow as the app's still renderer; `cirrus/media.py` imports `PIL`, confirming it is an intentional runtime dependency rather than a development-only tool.
A source-wide search found no Redis, MongoDB, MySQL, Celery/RQ, object-store, search, mail, OAuth, or identity-provider package references.

R21_scope_discipline.criterion: No module in the tree implements a capability the checklist never asked for: there is no cart, price or payment code, no comment, like, share, rating or view-counter store, no site-search index, no newsletter or mail sender, no chat widget and no second analytics library.
R21_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A module implements a capability when it defines a route, a table, a model or a service function for it, not when a word merely appears in a comment or in a copy string. Broad absence searches were corroborated by the live page's same-origin-only network activity. The only superficially related features are explicit exceptions or nonviolations: mailto contact links, generated share-card metadata, the site's own sessionStorage page-view counter, client-side studio palette filtering, and work-index reordering.
evidence: Inspected the delivered /app tree (58 files). cirrus/db.py defines only houses, accounts, items, media, credits, preview_tokens, and slug_redirects; there are no cart/payment/pricing, reactions/comments/ratings, search-index, newsletter/mail, chat, or analytics tables.

Route enumeration found only health/auth, works, talents, disciplines, media, preview, studio item-management, work reordering, preview-token, generated share-image, and public page routes. There is no site-search route, comments/reactions endpoint, commerce endpoint, mail-sending endpoint, or chat endpoint.

requirements.txt contains only Flask/Gunicorn/Postgres/template/Pillow support packages and no commerce, mail, chat, search, or analytics library. base.html loads only same-origin `/static/site.js` and `/static/alpine.min.js`; the live home-page network log recorded 26 requests to exactly one origin.

static/site.js implements only the site's own permitted page-view counter, storing daily counts under `cirrus_pv` in sessionStorage. No second analytics library, beacon, or analytics endpoint exists; source search found no Google Analytics, Segment, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Plausible, Matomo, Intercom, Drift, Crisp, Zendesk, or Tawk integration.

R22_scope_discipline.criterion: Every file in the tree is reached from a route table, a model, a template, a settings module or the seed module that a checklist obligation required; no framework scaffolding and no unreferenced helper survives unused.
R22_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A file is reached when a route table, a model, a template, a settings module, the seed module, or something itself reached imports, renders, extends, includes or links it; entry points, configuration files, migrations, the seed, USER_README.md and deployment files are reached by definition. Yes if every remaining source file in the tree is reached that way, template partials, stylesheets and scripts included. No if the tree carries framework scaffolding the checklist never asked for -- an unused blueprint, an empty admin or moderation module, a generated boilerplate view -- or a helper, template, stylesheet or script that nothing imports, renders or links.
R22_scope_discipline.rationale: R22 is false because at least two template partial files survive in the delivered tree without any route, reached template, or other reached source importing, extending, including, rendering, or linking them. The criterion is conjunctive and explicitly says an unreferenced template makes the answer No, so these direct source counterexamples resolve the criterion even though the rest of the tree is largely connected.
evidence: The delivered source tree contains `templates/partials/_counter.html` and `templates/partials/_tile.html`.
A source-wide regex search over `**/*` for `_counter\.html|partials/_counter|include ... partials/_counter` returned no matches in any of the 40 searchable source files.
A separate source-wide regex search over `**/*` for `_tile\.html|partials/_tile|include ... partials/_tile` likewise returned no matches.

The actual template dependency map shows routes rendered from `cirrus/pages.py` and error handlers, all page templates extending `base.html`, and referenced partials including `_marks.html`, `_contact_overlay.html`, `_footer.html`, `_caption.html`, `_work_body.html`, and `_talent_body.html`; neither `_counter.html` nor `_tile.html` appears in that map.

Static application files are reached from `base.html`: `/static/app.css`, `/static/site.js`, `/static/alpine.min.js`, and both font files are linked there; the stylesheet also references both fonts. Generated share media is reached by the `/share.jpg` route and `media.share_image()`. These checks reinforce that the two unused partials are specific surviving unreferenced files rather than a failure to identify the app entry graph.

R23_scope_discipline.criterion: No binary file is committed anywhere in the tree - no image, no moving-image file, no typeface file and no icon file - and every generated artwork routine derives its output in source from the seed stored on the record it belongs to.
R23_scope_discipline.evaluation_rule: A committed asset file is any image, moving-image, typeface or icon file present in the delivered source tree -- extensions such as .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .avif, .mp4, .webm, .mov, .woff, .woff2, .ttf, .otf, .ico, and a standalone .svg kept as its own file rather than written into the markup -- with node_modules and lockfiles excluded; vector geometry written inline in a template, SVG filter definitions and CSS gradients are not files and are never violations. Yes if no such file exists anywhere in the tree and the still and reel routines each derive their output in source from the seed stored on the media row they belong to. No if the tree carries a photograph, a placeholder or share image, a grain tile written out as a raster, a favicon, a sprite sheet, a video file, a typeface file, or a mark kept as a separate vector file, whether it sits in a static directory or in a generated-output directory that ships with the build, or if a still or reel routine reads pixels from a shipped file rather than deriving them from that row's stored seed.
R23_scope_discipline.rationale: The requirement is not met. Multiple forbidden binary assets ship in the delivered tree, including two font files and two generated raster files. Independently, the still renderer consumes the shipped grain raster when present, which violates the rule against reading shipped pixels instead of deriving the still entirely from its row seed. Although the reel canvas is procedurally driven by its media row seed and the main still gradient is seed-driven, the binary-file and still-grain violations conclusively make this conjunctive criterion false.
evidence: A complete delivered-tree listing (`source_list` at `/app`, depth 4) found committed binary assets: `static/fonts/CirrusDisplay-VF.woff2`, `static/fonts/CirrusText-VF.woff2`, `static/gen/grain-300.png`, and `static/gen/share-1200x630.jpg`. The criterion explicitly counts typefaces and generated-output images that ship with the build as violations.
The focused `static` tree listing confirmed those four binary files are physically present alongside the CSS/JS, rather than merely being runtime URL references.

`cirrus/db.py` defines `media.seed TEXT NOT NULL`. `cirrus/app.py` selects each media row's `m.seed` and invokes `media.render_still(row["seed"], row["width"], row["height"])`, while `cirrus/media.py` hashes the supplied seed in `_seed_int` and uses it in `_gradient_pair`; thus the principal still gradient is derived from its media row's stored seed.

However, the still routine also calls `grain_tile_image()`, and `cirrus/media.py` explicitly executes `Image.open(path).convert("L")` when `static/gen/grain-300.png` exists. Because that raster is present in the delivered tree, still rendering reads pixels from a shipped file rather than deriving all artwork from the row's stored seed—an explicit failure under the evaluation rule.

For reels, templates including `templates/partials/_work_body.html` and `_talent_body.html` place the reel media row's `seed` in `data-seed`; `static/site.js` reads `canvas.dataset.seed`, hashes all characters into `n`, and derives gradient direction, phase/shift, colours, and grain-point coordinates from that value each frame. This directly supports that the reel routine uses the seed on its own media row.

R24_internal_consistency.criterion: One naming scheme governs the whole tree: module names, model names, template file names and the context keys handed to those templates follow a single convention rather than one convention per surface.
R24_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: A naming convention is the casing and word form an identifier takes -- snake_case, kebab-case, CamelCase, singular or plural -- not the everyday word chosen for a thing. Prose, comments, user-facing copy and CSS class names are outside this criterion, and calling one entity an item in one place and a record or an entry in another is a vocabulary choice, not a second convention; the brief itself uses all three words, so that alone is never a violation. Yes if module file names, model or table names and template file names each follow one convention across the whole tree, and the context keys handed to templates follow one convention and name the same value the same way wherever that value is passed. No if template file names mix snake_case with kebab-case or CamelCase, if module file names mix conventions with each other, if models and their tables follow different conventions from one another, or if one and the same value reaches two templates under two different context keys.
R24_internal_consistency.rationale: Direct inspection of the complete delivered source establishes one naming form on each relevant surface: lowercase snake_case modules, plural lowercase snake_case tables (with no domain model layer), lowercase snake_case template files, and lowercase snake_case template context keys. Shared template values retain the same keys where reused. The apparent entity words `item`, `work`, and `talent` are vocabulary/domain-role distinctions and do not introduce a casing or word-form convention conflict under the evaluation rule.
evidence: The delivered source tree contains only lowercase/snake_case Python module filenames: cirrus/app.py, auth.py, db.py, media.py, pages.py, renderers.py, repo.py, seed.py, plus the conventional special file __init__.py; run.py is likewise lowercase. No kebab-case or CamelCase module filename appears in the complete 58-file tree listing.

cirrus/db.py defines all seven tables with one convention: plural lowercase snake_case (`houses`, `accounts`, `items`, `media`, `credits`, `preview_tokens`, `slug_redirects`). A whole-module class search found only utility/error classes (`ApiError`, `_Conn`, `Pool`, `_PoolFacade`, `_Random`) and no separate domain/ORM model layer whose names could conflict with the tables.

All template filenames in the complete tree use lowercase snake_case: single-word names such as `entry.html`, `works.html`, `talent.html`, and studio names such as `published.html`; multiword partials consistently use snake_case with the conventional partial prefix, e.g. `_contact_overlay.html`, `_talent_body.html`, and `_work_body.html`. A source-wide search found no CamelCase `.html` name and no kebab-case `.html` name.

The exhaustive `render_template`/`_view` call search found all template handoffs in cirrus/pages.py, cirrus/app.py, and cirrus/__init__.py. Their context keys consistently use lowercase snake_case: common keys `title`, `description`, `share_image`, `account`, `house`, `route_name`; route keys including `works`, `stills`, `work`, `ordinal`, `media`, `gallery`, `reel`, `poster`, `credits`, `prev`, `nxt`, `talents`, `disciplines`, `active_discipline`, `talents_json`, `disciplines_json`, `poster_by_

Repeated values retain their established context keys across handoffs: `account`, `house`, and `route_name` are centralized in `_view`; talent collections remain `talents`; selected-work media remains `selected_media` in both talent detail and preview; work-detail components remain `ordinal`, `media`, `gallery`, `reel`, `poster`, `credits`, `prev`, and `nxt` when reused by preview. No mixed-casing alias was found.

R25_internal_consistency.criterion: The house-scoping decision is written once as one reusable unit of source that every studio read path and every studio write path applies, rather than restated inline in each handler.
R25_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: The house-scoping decision is the rule that a studio caller reaches only records whose house matches their own account's house, and that a foreign record is answered exactly as a missing one. Yes if that rule is written once -- a single decorator, dependency, query helper or base query -- and every studio read path and every studio write path reaches its record through it. No if two or more studio handlers each carry their own inline house comparison, if the read paths use one mechanism and the write paths another, or if any studio handler loads a record without passing through that single unit.
R25_internal_consistency.rationale: The source does enforce house isolation in many places, and `own_item` gives foreign and missing item IDs the same 404 for several API handlers. However, the criterion is specifically single ownership of that decision across every studio read and write path. The delivered source restates and applies house scoping through multiple mechanisms, including multiple inline predicates, so the criterion is definitively not satisfied.
evidence: Delivered source `cirrus/app.py` defines two different reusable units: `require_house()` obtains the producer's house, while `own_item(item_id)` calls `require_house()` and then `repo.item_by_id(item_id, house_id)`, returning the same 404 `ApiError("Not found")` for an inaccessible item.

The API studio collection read `studio_items` (lines 305–323) calls `require_house()` and restates scoping in its own SQL as `FROM items WHERE house_id = %s`; the record read `studio_item` instead calls `own_item(item_id)`. Thus even studio reads do not all reach records through one shared scoping unit.

API writes also split mechanisms: record-specific writes `studio_patch`, `studio_publish`, `studio_media`, `studio_credit`, and `studio_slug` call `own_item(item_id)`, while `studio_create`, `studio_order`, and `studio_preview_tokens` call `require_house()` and perform separate house-scoped queries/checks. `studio_order` has its own `SELECT id FROM items WHERE house_id = %s ...` and house predicate on update; `studio_preview_tokens` directly calls `repo.item_by_id(..., house_id)`.

Server-rendered studio reads in `cirrus/pages.py` use yet another pattern: `_guard()` checks producer/house, `/studio` and `/studio/*/new` contain inline `WHERE house_id = %s` queries, and `/studio/items/<id>` plus its `/published` page call `repo.item_by_id(item_id, acct["house_id"])` directly rather than a single shared record-scoping guard.

Source-wide route searches found 10 `/api/studio...` handlers and 6 `/studio...` page handlers, while usage search showed the above mixture of `own_item`, `require_house`, `_guard`, direct `repo.item_by_id`, and inline `house_id` SQL predicates. This directly violates the rule that every studio read and write path apply one reusable house-scoping decision.

R26_internal_consistency.criterion: The four derived values - the read-time ordinal, the discipline set, a talent's selected work and a work's neighbours - are each computed by one helper the whole tree calls, and none of the four is also held as a stored column.
R26_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: The four derived values are the displayed ordinal, the roster's discipline set, a talent's selected work, and a work's neighbours. Yes if each is computed by exactly one helper that every caller in the tree uses, and none of the four is also persisted. No if any of the four is recomputed inline in a second module, route or template, if two helpers compute the same value, or if the schema carries a stored ordinal, discipline-set, selected-work or neighbour column, index or cache holding one of them.
R26_internal_consistency.rationale: The persistence half is satisfied, and discipline-set plus selected-work each have a single shared repository helper. But the criterion is conjunctive and explicitly says No if any value is recomputed inline in a second route/module. Both the displayed ordinal and work neighbours are independently recomputed in pages.py in addition to repo.py, with further duplication in preview/published paths. Therefore R26 is not satisfied.
evidence: Delivered schema in cirrus/db.py defines only houses, accounts, items, media, credits, preview_tokens, and slug_redirects. There is no ordinal, roster discipline-set, selected-work, or neighbour column/index/cache; selected work is represented by the underlying credits.talent_item_id relationship, and items.discipline is the per-talent source field rather than a stored roster set.

cirrus/repo.py has one discipline_set() helper, and source-wide search found its only callers at cirrus/pages.py:99 and cirrus/app.py:235. It also has one selected_works() helper, with callers at pages.py:129, pages.py:277, and app.py:227.

The ordinal violates single computation ownership: cirrus/repo.py:8-12 defines _ordinals(), but cirrus/pages.py independently recomputes the displayed value with `"%03d" % (idx + 1)` at line 89, repeats equivalent computation at lines 229 and 266, and passes those values to work/published/preview templates. Source search found six `%03d` occurrences, including these independent page computations.

Work neighbours also violate single computation ownership: repo.work_by_slug() derives prev/next at repo.py:69-70, while pages.work_detail independently derives them from published_works at pages.py:82-83, and the preview route repeats the neighbour indexing at pages.py:270-271.

Runtime reconciliation on the first listed work showed ordinal 001 for The Halo and its detail showed PREVIOUS Probe Work 5c9354efb62c / NEXT Sonder, matching the ordered list's wraparound and next entry; however, source proves those displayed values are produced by the duplicate inline page logic rather than one tree-wide helper.

R27_internal_consistency.criterion: The thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal identifier that media rows and preview tokens both carry is minted by a single helper every model calls, so the convention has one definition in source rather than a repeated literal per table.
R27_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: The identifier is the thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal token carried by the media row's id and by the preview token's token column. Yes if one helper mints it and both models call that helper, so the length, the case and the alphabet have one definition in source. No if each model builds its own token with its own uuid4 hex, token_hex or urandom expression, if the minting length literal appears at more than one site, or if the two tables mint by different routines.
R27_internal_consistency.rationale: The requirement is not met. Media IDs are minted through `db.new_id()`, while preview token values are independently minted with a direct `secrets.token_hex(16)` call in the API module. Therefore both values have the expected practical format, but the length/alphabet convention does not have a single minting definition and the `16` length argument is repeated at two source sites, which the evaluation rule explicitly classifies as a failure.
evidence: `cirrus/db.py` defines `new_id()` as `return secrets.token_hex(16)`, establishing one 32-character lowercase hexadecimal minting site.
`cirrus/app.py` creates media IDs with `media_id = db.new_id()` before inserting them into `media`, so media rows use the database helper.

`cirrus/app.py` separately creates preview tokens with `token = secrets.token_hex(16)` before inserting them into `preview_tokens`; it does not call `db.new_id()` (or another shared identifier helper) for the token column.
A source-wide grep for `token_hex\(16\)` found exactly two minting sites: `cirrus/db.py:99` and `cirrus/app.py:595`. Thus the minting expression and its length literal are repeated.
The schema in `cirrus/db.py` constrains `preview_tokens.token` with `CHECK (token ~ '^[0-9a-f]{32}$')`, confirming the token convention being evaluated.

R28_internal_consistency.criterion: Instants are held in UTC and a slug is lowercased at one boundary before it is stored or compared, and both conventions are applied identically in every model, seed routine and serialiser that touches them.
R28_internal_consistency.evaluation_rule: An instant is any stored or serialised timestamp -- created_at, published_at, expires_at -- and the boundary is the single place a slug is normalised. Yes if every timestamp is produced and stored in UTC through one convention, a slug is lowercased once at that one boundary before it is stored or compared, and every model, seed routine and serialiser applies both conventions identically. No if some modules take a naive local-time now while others take a UTC-aware one, if a slug is lowercased in a route handler in one place and in a model or the seed in another, or if any lookup compares a slug without lowercasing, so that Rives and rives could diverge.
R28_internal_consistency.rationale: The requirement is conjunctive and explicitly says it fails if any lookup compares a slug without lowercasing. Both direct behavior and source prove that uppercase `Rives` and lowercase `rives` diverge because read paths do not use the central slug normalizer. UTC instant handling appears consistent, but the failed slug convention is sufficient to make R28 false.
evidence: Direct runtime comparison: GET /api/talents/rives returned HTTP 200 with slug "rives", while GET /api/talents/Rives returned HTTP 404. Likewise, /talents/rives returned the Rives page and /talents/Rives returned 404. Thus the same logical slug diverges by case during lookup.

Delivered source confirms the cause in cirrus/repo.py: work_by_slug and talent_by_slug compare `r["slug"] == slug`, and resolve_slug queries `slug = %s` / `old_slug = %s`, without normalizing the lookup argument.
